content: 1. Ferris DG and Miller MD conducted a study in 1993 to evaluate the accuracy of colposcopy within a residency training program. Their research aimed to define the levels of competency and proficiency required for effective colposcopic diagnosis. The findings were published in the Journal of Family Practice. 2. Homesley HD, Jobson VW, and Reish RL, in 1984, investigated the use of colposcopically directed, four-quadrant cervical biopsies performed by colposcopy trainees. This study was published in the Journal of Reproductive Medicine and provided insights into the diagnostic utility of this approach in training settings. 3. Jones DE and colleagues, in 1987, evaluated the clinical implications of atypical Pap smear results. Their findings, published in the American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology, highlighted the diagnostic challenges and subsequent management strategies for atypical cytological findings. 4. Kierkegaard O and colleagues, in 1994, assessed the diagnostic accuracy of cytology and colposcopy in detecting cervical squamous intraepithelial lesions. Their research, published in Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica, provided critical data on the sensitivity and specificity of these diagnostic tools. 5. Mousavi AS and colleagues conducted a prospective study in 2007 to evaluate the correlation between the Reid colposcopic index impressions and biopsy histology. Their findings, published in the Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease, demonstrated the clinical utility of the Reid index in guiding colposcopic assessments. 6. Patil K and colleagues, in 2011, compared the diagnostic efficacy of visual inspection of the cervix with acetic acid (VIA) and Pap smear testing for cervical cancer prevention. Their study, published in the Journal of South Asian Federation of Obstetrics and Gynecology (SAFOG), explored whether VIA could potentially replace the Pap smear in resource-limited settings. 7. Denny L and colleagues, in 2008, examined the relationship between human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical disease in women infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1). Their findings, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, underscored the increased risk of cervical disease in this population. 8. De Vuyst H and colleagues, in 2008, explored the interplay between HIV, HPV, and cervical neoplasia in the context of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Their research, published in the European Journal of Cancer Prevention, highlighted the implications of co-infection on cervical cancer risk. 9. De Vuyst H and colleagues also investigated the prevalence and determinants of HPV infection and cervical lesions in HIV-positive women in Kenya. Their findings, published in the British Journal of Cancer, provided valuable epidemiological data for this high-risk population. 10. Joshi S and colleagues, in 2013, conducted a study on cervical neoplasia screening in HIV-infected women in India. Their research, published in AIDS, emphasized the importance of tailored screening strategies for this vulnerable group. 11. The Osmanabad District Cervical Screening Study Group conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial in 2005 to compare visual inspection, cytology, and HPV screening for cervical cancer in rural India. Their findings, published in the International Journal of Cancer, provided evidence for the feasibility and effectiveness of these screening methods in low-resource settings. 12. Zhang HY and colleagues, in 2012, conducted a pilot study to assess HPV prevalence and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia among HIV-infected women in Yunnan Province, China. Their findings, published in the Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention, highlighted the burden of cervical disease in this population. 13. The expert panel recommends a screening strategy involving an HPV test followed by VIA and treatment with cryotherapy (or LEEP if cryotherapy is not feasible). Alternatively, a single HPV test followed by treatment with cryotherapy (or LEEP) is also suggested. This recommendation is conditional and based on low-quality evidence. The panel notes that reductions in cervical cancer incidence and mortality are greater with a single HPV test compared to HPV testing followed by VIA. However, the single-test approach may lead to overtreatment and associated harms. The panel also highlights the resource implications of implementing a two-step strategy, including the need for additional training and follow-up visits. 14. Evidence for the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing followed by VIA compared to HPV testing alone is of low to very low quality. Observational studies on treatment effects and the natural progression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) often yield inconsistent results, leading to uncertainty in linking test accuracy data to treatment outcomes. 15. The balance of benefits versus harms and burdens suggests that HPV testing followed by VIA may result in fewer major harms due to reduced overtreatment. However, it may also lead to slightly higher detection rates of cervical cancer and CIN recurrence. In HIV-positive women, the benefits of screening are more pronounced, but there is also a higher risk of CIN recurrence and cervical cancer-related mortality with HPV testing followed by VIA compared to HPV testing alone. 16. High value is placed on a screen-and-treat strategy compared to no screening, as qualitative studies indicate that women find screening tests and immediate treatment acceptable once they decide to participate. Reducing overtreatment and associated complications is also highly valued. 17. Resource implications indicate that HPV testing followed by VIA may require greater resources due to the additional test. However, this approach may reduce overtreatment and associated complications, potentially offsetting some of the resource demands. 18. The diagnostic test accuracy of HPV testing followed by VIA compared to HPV testing alone in HIV-positive women is based on moderate-quality evidence. The sensitivity and specificity of the tests vary, and the absolute differences in true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives are noted. 19. The GRADE evidence for patient-important outcomes following different screen-and-treat strategies highlights the trade-offs between mortality reduction, cancer detection, and treatment-related complications. The desirability of outcomes varies depending on the strategy employed, with HPV testing alone or followed by VIA showing different profiles of benefits and harms. 20. The expert panel emphasizes the importance of considering the context, including resource availability and population-specific factors, when implementing cervical cancer screening strategies. The recommendations are conditional and should be adapted to local settings to maximize benefits and minimize harms.
